# Space travel-associated motion sickness and its treatment

## Abstract

Lan received support from NASA grant 80NSSC22K0847, which is focused on

means that maintaining peak performance and avoiding, or at least minimizing, undesirable medication side effects are core priorities. On an airplane ride or boat cruise the sedative side effects of an antimotion sickness drug might be welcome, but on a space mission, and in many military situations, these drug side effects can impair job performance. Several approaches exist to minimize side effects while maximizing the effectiveness of antimotion sickness drugs. Choosing drugs with a narrow and low-severity side effect profile is ideal. In situations where drug side effects cannot be avoided, administering an additional drug to combat the undesirable side effects is a possible strategy. Lastly, if routes of administration that provide a rapid onset of drug action can be used, the drug can be given just when it is needed, providing some confidence that the benefits of the drug will outweigh the risks of adverse events. Another important consideration is the primary goal of motion sickness treatment. Preventing vomiting is often desirable, such as in a space suit, but motion sickness symptoms include more than just vomiting. Motion sickness itself produces side effects such as nausea, malaise and drowsiness, which can reduce job performance.

Eliminating these symptoms in addition to preventing vomiting is often a key goal of treatment.

Several publications already exist that cover the main issues with space motion sickness. [1] [2] 2] [3] This article details the main drug classes typically used in motion sickness treatment, discusses the pros and cons of different modes of administration, presents the main drugs used in space and reviews new developments in the field.

## | Neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists

Neurokinin-1 (NK-1) receptors are found in the brainstem and gastrointestinal tract and are involved in the regulation of vomiting. Figure 1 illustrates the locations of NK-1 receptors and other receptors relevant to motion sickness therapy. Drugs that inhibit NK-1 receptors (NK-1 antagonists, such as aprepitant) are useful for preventing vomiting produced by cancer chemotherapy. 4, 5 Their use in treating motion sickness is more problematic. A recent study with tradipitant for seasickness showed that while it reduced vomiting significantly, it did not have a significant effect on the motion sickness severity score. 6 Earlier studies with an NK-1 antagonist alone or in combination with a 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 receptor (5-HT 3 ) antagonist also did not show efficacy in improving motion sickness symptoms. 7 vertheless, these drugs may be useful for preventing vomiting even if they may not relieve the other symptoms of motion sickness.

## | Acetylcholine muscarinic receptor antagonists

Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are located within the vestibular system (Figure 1 ) and anticholinergic agents that work as antagonists at muscarinic receptors are effective for treating motion sickness. 1, 8 ere are five subtypes of muscarinic receptors (M 1 -M 5 ). Scopolamine, the drug with the longest history and best efficacy in treating motion sickness, is an antagonist at all five. Promethazine, another drug often used for space motion sickness, also is an antagonist at all five muscarinic receptors. There has been interest in finding muscarinic antagonists that target specific subtypes of muscarinic receptors.

Golding et al compared the M 3 specific antagonist darifenacin to scopolamine and found that while darifenacin had few cognitive effects, it was not effective for treating motion sickness. 9 Studies in a cat model of motion sickness have shown that inhibiting the M 1 and M 2 receptors may not be useful for treating motion sickness, 10 instead inhibiting the M 4 and M 5 receptors may be most important for motion sickness treatment. 9 Currently, no approved specific antagonists for these muscarinic receptor subtypes are available.

## | Histamine receptor antagonists

Histamine receptors have four subtypes (H 1 -H 4 ), but H 1 receptors are the ones thought to be most important in the pathophysiology of motion sickness. H 1 receptors are found in the vestibular system and related areas that process balance information (Figure 1 ). Most of the antihistamines effective in treating motion sickness, such as diphenhydramine or meclizine, also cause considerable sedation. To avoid the sedative effects of antihistamines, nonsedating antihistamines that cross the blood-brain barrier to a lesser extent than the more sedating first-generation antihistamines have been developed (such as cetirizine). These non-sedating antihistamines unfortunately are not effective against motion sickness, 11 likely because the antihistamines must act centrally to reduce motion sickness. Also, many of the firstgeneration antihistamines are pleotropic in their receptor antagonist activity. Diphenhydramine, for example, also has antimuscarinic properties. Similarly, drugs that are classified as primarily muscarinic antagonists may act at histamine receptors as well. For example, promethazine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist, but it is also an antagonist at the histamine receptor.

## | Adrenergic receptor agonists

Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors exist in the vestibular nuclei (Figure 1 ) and may provide a potential site of action for sympathomimetics like ephedrine or dexamphetamine. 12 Although these drugs are most commonly used in motion sickness treatment to combat the sedative side effects of other drugs (like scopolamine or promethazine), they are effective against motion sickness in humans as single agents. 8,13 receptor antagonists are effective at reducing vomiting in several clinical settings (eg, cancer chemotherapy) but are not effective for motion sickness. The most effective current motion sickness drugs act at the muscarinic and histaminic receptors.

## | Summary of other drug classes with antimotion sickness potential

Other classes of drugs aside from the ones detailed above may have some effects on motion sickness. Some natural therapies have been recommended, such as high-dose vitamin C and ginger. 14 The drugs detailed above, however, are the most well established and widely studied. ## | ROUTE OF ADMINISTRATION

Antimotion sickness drugs are effective when given orally, but once motion sickness symptoms begin, absorption of orally administered drugs is reduced substantially, 15 therefore orally administered motion sickness drugs must be given well in advance of symptom onset because they are largely ineffective once motion sickness symptoms have developed. This presents a challenge for managing motion sickness in space. If medications are given pre-mission to prevent motion sickness, some individuals will experience significant drug side effects while in space (eg, sedation, reduced attention, urinary retention) even though they might not have developed severe motion sickness symptoms if left unmedicated. If oral medications are postponed until symptoms develop during spaceflight, it is likely they might not be absorbed adequately to be effective.

In the Space Shuttle program, the solution to this problem was using intramuscular injections of promethazine. 16 This approach provided rapid motion sickness relief with a generally acceptable sideeffect profile. 17 Injections provide a rapid onset of drug effect but require needles and training, which makes them undesirable in some operational settings. Motion sickness tends to occur in the early part of space missions and again on landing when the vestibular system is readjusting to the Earth's gravity. Crew members may still be in spacesuits during these times and after landing they may be in a capsule that is in motion on the sea. Giving an injection in those settings is difficult, which has prompted the investigation of alternative administration routes.

Intranasal administration is an attractive option because an intranasal drug could be self-administered and the delivery device could be easily stored in a pocket on a spacesuit or within a space capsule. Several of the drugs listed in Table 1 have been administered intranasally in humans, such as scopolamine, ephedrine and amphetamine. [18] [19] [20] Intranasal promethazine has been studied in an animal model. 21 Of the drugs listed in Table 1 , the one that has been most studied for treating motion sickness as an intranasal preparation is scopolamine.

Scopolamine has a low dose requirement for treating motion sickness (0.4-0.6 mg), which makes it attractive for administration via alternative routes. For example, buccal scopolamine administration has been tested to prevent motion sickness in parabolic flight with good results. 22 3 | ROUTE OF ADMINISTRATION

## | HABITUATION

Perhaps the most effective treatment for motion sickness is time.

Almost all motion sickness drug use occurs within the first couple of days of a spaceflight. Over time, individuals habituate to weightlessness and the risk and prevalence of motion sickness decreases, only to reappear after landing when a readaptation to Earth's gravity takes place. Unfortunately, for some commercial spaceflights the bulk of the journey occurs during the time when there is a high risk of motion sickness and individuals do not have time to adapt fully.

Since habituation to motion sickness is so important, drugs that interfere with habituation would be less desirable on longer missions.

A failure to habituate would increase the amount of antimotion sickness drug use and might allow for motion sickness symptoms to persist longer into a mission, where they could interfere with extravehicular activities or other operational tasks.
